sermon:
# The Beginning of the Gospel
## Mark 1:1-45

Matthew opens with a genealogy. Luke opens with two pregnancies and a song. John opens before time itself. Mark opens with a man standing in a river, and before that, with a sentence that does not argue. He announces. "The beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God" (Mark 1:1). There is no warm-up. There is no case being built toward a conclusion. The conclusion comes first, and the rest of the book will ask whether you can bear to believe it.

**A verdict, not an argument**

The word translated gospel was not a religious word. It was a word Rome used when a new emperor was enthroned, good news of a new power in the world. Mark takes that word and hands it to a carpenter from Nazareth. Then he quotes Isaiah and the wilderness fills with people going out to be baptized, confessing, waiting for someone the Baptist says he is not worthy to unstrap a sandal for. When Jesus comes up from the water the heavens are torn open, the word Mark uses for violence, and a voice claims him as a beloved Son. The verdict of verse one is confirmed from above before a single miracle is performed.

Then the Spirit drives him into the wilderness, and out of it he comes preaching: "The time is fulfilled, and the kingdom of God is at hand; repent, and believe in the gospel" (Mark 1:15). Everything that follows in chapter one is what it looks like when the kingdom arrives. He calls fishermen and they leave their nets in mid-sentence. He silences a demon that knows his name. He heals a fever, a leper, a town's worth of sick at the door by sundown.

**Everyone sees but the crowds**

Notice who recognizes him. The demons know exactly who he is and he silences them. The leper, cleansed, cannot stop talking. But the crowds gather for the wrong reason. By the end of the chapter Jesus cannot enter a town openly because the demand for healing has buried the announcement of the kingdom. They want the works. They do not want the King.

That is the temptation that has never left the church. We will take the benefits of Jesus and decline his rule. We will pray for the fever to break and resent the call to leave the net. I have done this. I have wanted the door at sundown crowded with my answered prayers and gone quiet when the same Lord said repent. Mark will not let me hold the miracles and drop the kingdom. The two arrive together or not at all.

**The Christ connection**

The One announced in verse one as Son of God will be confessed as Son of God in only one other place in this Gospel, by a Roman soldier at the foot of a cross. Mark is telling you from the first line where the authority of chapter one is heading. The hand that touched the leper, which under the law should have made Jesus unclean, instead made the leper clean. That reversal is the whole gospel in miniature. He takes our defilement and gives us his cleanness. The cross is where the exchange is finished.

The beginning of the gospel is not your decision. It is his arrival. He has already come near, already torn the heavens, already called you by name from across the water. The only question Mark leaves on the bank is whether you will follow, or stay in the crowd that wanted only the cure.

The kingdom has come near.

# The Authority They Could Not Forgive
## Mark 2:1-3:6

A crowd packs a house in Capernaum so tightly that four men carrying a paralyzed friend cannot get through the door. So they go up on the roof, dig through it, and lower the man down on his mat into the room where Jesus is teaching. It is a desperate, almost comic scene, dirt falling, a stretcher descending. And then Jesus says the one thing nobody came for. Not "be healed." "Son, your sins are forgiven" (Mark 2:5).

**Five collisions**

Mark stacks five conflicts back to back, and they escalate. First the forgiveness of the paralytic, where the scribes think, rightly, that only God can forgive sins, and Jesus answers their unspoken charge by healing the man as proof of an authority they cannot see. Then he calls Levi the tax collector and eats with sinners, and the keepers of the law ask why. Then his disciples do not fast. Then they pluck grain on the Sabbath. Then he heals a withered hand on the Sabbath in the synagogue itself, looking around, Mark says, with anger and grief at their hardness of heart.

Each collision is the same collision. Jesus keeps claiming what belongs to God alone. He forgives sins. He declares himself Lord of the Sabbath, the institution God gave at creation. "The Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath. So the Son of Man is lord even of the Sabbath" (Mark 2:27-28). He is not bending the rules. He is announcing that he stands over them, because he is the one who gave them.

**An authority too absolute to permit**

Here is what the religious leaders understood that many comfortable readers miss. They were not wrong that this was a staggering claim. They were wrong about what to do with it. They reasoned correctly that no mere teacher may forgive sins or master the Sabbath, and then they drew the lethal conclusion. If we cannot make him fit under our authority, he must be removed. By the last verse of this section the Pharisees go out and conspire with the Herodians, their political enemies, on how to destroy him. The defenders of the law have decided to break the sixth commandment to protect their version of the rest.

This is the religion that cannot forgive a Savior for being a Savior. It would rather guard its hand on the law than receive forgiveness as a gift through the door it did not control. I know this religion from the inside. There is a version of me that prefers to be the one who measures sin rather than the one who is forgiven of it, who would sooner manage God than be undone by him. The withered hand in the synagogue is mine. He says stretch it out. The Pharisee in me would rather keep it curled and call it reverence.

**The Christ connection**

Which is the easier thing, to say your sins are forgiven, or to say rise and walk? It is easy to say the first because no one can check it. So Jesus heals the body to prove the harder, invisible thing is true. But there is a cost behind that claim, and Mark has already told us where it lands. The plot to destroy him in chapter three is the first tremor of Calvary. He could announce forgiveness with a word in Capernaum only because he would purchase it with his blood in Jerusalem. The authority they could not forgive is the authority that came to forgive them, and would die so the room full of paralytics could walk out free.

They plotted to destroy him.

# Naming the True Family
## Mark 3:7-35

There is a particular pain in being misunderstood by the people who raised you. Mark records it plainly. Jesus is so pressed by crowds that he cannot eat, and when his family hears, they go out to seize him, saying, "He is out of his mind" (Mark 3:21). The Greek is blunt. They came to take custody of him, the way you would restrain someone who has lost himself. The people who shared his table now think he has lost his reason.

**Two verdicts on Jesus**

Mark frames this section with two charges, and they bracket the same scene. From outside Galilee, the scribes come down and render their verdict: "He is possessed by Beelzebul, and by the prince of demons he casts out the demons" (Mark 3:22). From inside his own household comes the other: he is mad. The enemies say he is demonic. The family says he is deranged. Both have decided that the power at work in him cannot be the power of God.

Between these two charges Mark sets the appointment of the Twelve. Jesus goes up the mountain and calls those he desired, and they came to him, and he makes twelve to be with him and to be sent out. He is building something. While the scribes accuse and the family panics, he is constituting a new people around himself. The shape of the chapter is the argument of the chapter.

**A house divided and a sin not forgiven**

To the scribes Jesus answers with logic that closes every exit. How can Satan cast out Satan? A kingdom divided against itself cannot stand. No one plunders a strong man's house without first binding the strong man. He is the one binding Satan, and they are watching liberation and calling it the devil's work. Then comes the most frightening sentence in the chapter, the warning about blasphemy against the Holy Spirit that will not be forgiven. The eternal danger is not weakness or doubt. It is looking at the rescuing Spirit of God and calling him unclean, the settled refusal to receive grace as grace.

**Who counts as family**

Then the scene closes the bracket. His mother and brothers arrive, standing outside, sending word. And Jesus looks around at those seated in a circle near him and says it: "Whoever does the will of God, he is my brother and sister and mother" (Mark 3:35). He does not disown Mary. He redefines kinship. Blood does not make you his. Doing the will of God does.

This is harder than it sounds, and more tender. Harder, because it means proximity is not belonging. You can grow up in the house, eat at the table, carry the name, and stand outside. I have trusted my church background the way his brothers trusted their blood, as if nearness were the same as obedience. It is not. More tender, because it means the circle is open to anyone who will do the Father's will. The orphan, the outsider, the one with no family worth claiming, is offered a brother in Jesus and a Father in God.

**The Christ connection**

Jesus could form a new family only because he was willing to be torn from his own. The Son who endured being called mad and demonic was making a household for people who deserved neither his name nor his table. At the cross he would give his mother to a disciple and a disciple to his mother, the new family taking shape under the very weight that misunderstood him. He stood outside our belonging so we could be seated in the circle.

Doing God's will makes family.

# The Word Sown and the Wind Stilled
## Mark 4:1-41

A man scatters seed by hand across a field, and it lands where it lands. Some on the path, eaten by birds. Some on rocky ground, up fast and burned faster. Some among thorns, choked. Some on good soil, thirtyfold, sixtyfold, a hundredfold. Jesus tells this from a boat to a crowd on the shore, and then, alone with the Twelve, he explains that the seed is the word and the soils are hearts. The parable is not mainly about farming. It is about why the same announcement of the kingdom lands so differently in the people who hear it.

**Why the word does not take**

This is the question chapter four answers. The kingdom has come near, Jesus has been preaching, and yet the crowds want only the cures and the scribes call him demonic and his family thinks him mad. Why does the same word produce such different results? Because the word falls on different ground. Some hear and Satan snatches it. Some receive it with joy and have no root, so when tribulation comes they fall away. Some let the cares of the world and the deceitfulness of riches choke it dead. And some hear and accept and bear fruit.

The sobering thing is that three of the four soils fail. Hearing the word is not the same as keeping it. Jesus follows with the lamp that must not be hidden and the warning, "with the measure you use, it will be measured to you" (Mark 4:24). How you receive the word determines how much of it you are given. Then two seed parables of hope: the kingdom grows secretly while the farmer sleeps, and it starts smaller than a mustard seed and becomes the largest of garden plants. Hidden and small now. Vast at the harvest.

**The same word silences the storm**

Then Mark does something deliberate. The chapter of the word ends with a demonstration of the word. Evening comes, they cross the sea, a great storm breaks, and the boat is filling. Jesus is asleep on a cushion. They wake him, half accusing: do you not care that we are perishing? And he rises and speaks three syllables to the wind and the sea, "Peace, be still," and there is a dead calm. The same authoritative word that the soils received so unevenly now silences a storm that no fisherman could.

The disciples are left with the question the whole chapter has been forcing toward: "Who then is this, that even the wind and the sea obey him?" (Mark 4:41). The word that grows kingdoms in hidden soil is the word that commands the chaos. They are the same word, because they are the same Lord.

**The honest application**

I would like to think I am the good soil. But the thorns Jesus names are not gross sins. They are cares, riches, desires for other things, the ordinary furniture of a respectable life. The word does not usually die in me by violence. It dies by crowding. I let the anxieties of the week and the wanting of more grow up around it until there is no fruit, and I would not even notice the strangling if Jesus had not named it. That is the costly part. The thorn-soil heart looks busy and fruitful from the outside.

**The Christ connection**

The Sower scattered the word knowing most would not take, and then went out himself to die as the seed that falls into the ground. He stilled the storm on the sea, and he would face a greater storm on the cross, where the wrath we deserved broke over him and he did not say peace to it. He bore it, so that the word sown in us could finally bear fruit it never could on its own.

Even wind and sea obey.

# Authority Over What We Cannot Touch
## Mark 5:1-43

There are three people in this chapter that the world had given up on. A man no one could come near, a woman no one was allowed to touch, and a girl already past help. Mark puts them in a row on purpose. By the end of the chapter you understand that there is no place too far gone for the authority of Jesus, no chain, no defilement, no grave.

**The man no chains could hold**

He lives among the tombs in the country of the Gerasenes, a man whom no one could bind anymore, not even with chains, crying out night and day, cutting himself with stones. When Jesus steps off the boat the demons recognize him at once and beg not to be tormented. Their name is Legion, for they are many. Jesus sends them into a herd of pigs that rushes down the bank and drowns, and the townspeople come and find the man "sitting there, clothed and in his right mind" (Mark 5:15). And they are afraid, and they beg Jesus to leave. The healing terrifies them more than the demoniac did.

**The woman twelve years unclean**

Back across the sea, a synagogue ruler named Jairus falls at his feet because his little daughter is dying. On the way, in the crush of the crowd, a woman who has had a flow of blood for twelve years, who has spent everything on physicians and only grown worse, comes up behind and touches his garment. Under the law that flow made her perpetually unclean, and everything she touched unclean with her. She has lived twelve years untouchable. She touches him in secret and is healed, and Jesus stops everything to find her, not to shame her but to name her: "Daughter, your faith has made you well; go in peace" (Mark 5:34). The contact that should have defiled him instead cured her.

**The girl already mourned**

Then word comes that Jairus's daughter has died. Why trouble the Teacher further? And Jesus says to the father the words that hold this whole chapter together: "Do not fear, only believe" (Mark 5:36). He enters the house of mourning, puts out the wailing crowd, takes the dead girl by the hand, the hand of a corpse, and says, "Talitha cumi," little girl, arise. And she gets up and walks, and he tells them to give her something to eat. Twelve years of bleeding ended; twelve years of life restored. Mark sets the numbers side by side.

**What this asks of us**

Notice the order of his reach. He frees the demon-possessed, heals the ceremonially defiled, and raises the dead, and his power is not diminished by any of it. Where we expect contamination to flow toward him, cleansing flows out of him instead. But notice also the two responses. The townspeople, seeing his power over evil, beg him to go away. Jairus, with nothing left, is told only to believe. I am closer to the townspeople than I would like to admit. There is a part of me that finds an undisturbed life with my own small demons more comfortable than the disruption of a Lord who actually casts them out. Real authority is not safe. It changes the neighborhood.

**The Christ connection**

The One who took the unclean woman's defilement and the dead girl's corpse-hand without being defiled is the One who would take all our uncleanness onto himself at the cross and not be overcome by it. He touched the grave here and reversed it; he would enter the grave himself and break it open. To every father at the edge of a sickbed, to everyone unclean for too many years, to everyone living among the tombs, his word is the same.

Do not fear, only believe.

# Who Do You Say I Am
## Mark 6:30-44; 8:1-30

Twice Jesus feeds a multitude in the wilderness from almost nothing. The first time, five thousand men from five loaves and two fish, with twelve baskets of fragments left over. The second time, four thousand from seven loaves, with seven baskets gathered. And both times the disciples stand in front of impossible math and ask the same despairing question: where would we get bread for these in a desolate place? They have already watched him do it once. They ask again as if it never happened.

**The bread they could not read**

Mark is not impressed by the size of the crowds. He is tracking the disciples' hearts. After the first feeding they cross the sea, Jesus walks on the water, and Mark says they were utterly astounded, "for they did not understand about the loaves, but their hearts were hardened" (Mark 6:52). The bread was a sign, and they missed the sign. Later, in the boat, when they worry that they forgot to bring bread, Jesus is exasperated: do you not yet perceive? Having eyes do you not see? Do you not remember the baskets? The bread was never the point. The point was the one breaking it.

Right before Caesarea Philippi, Mark places a strange two-stage healing. Jesus touches a blind man, who then sees men like trees walking, and only after a second touch does he see clearly. It is the only miracle Jesus does in stages, and Mark sets it like a parable of the disciples themselves. They are beginning to see. They are not yet seeing clearly. They need a second touch.

**The hinge of the whole book**

Then they come to the villages of Caesarea Philippi, and Jesus asks the question that the loaves and the storms and the parables have all been driving toward. First the easy version: who do people say that I am? John the Baptist, Elijah, one of the prophets. Then the version that costs something: "But who do you say that I am?" Peter answers for them all: "You are the Christ" (Mark 8:29). After thousands of verses of the question, who then is this, someone finally says it out loud.

This is the hinge on which the Gospel of Mark turns. Everything before this has been asking the question. Everything after this will redefine the answer. Because the moment Peter confesses him as Christ, Jesus begins to teach plainly that the Son of Man must suffer many things, be rejected, killed, and after three days rise. Peter rebukes him for it. Peter has the right title and the wrong picture. He confesses a Christ of glory and recoils from a Christ of the cross.

**Where this leaves us**

It is possible to give the correct answer about Jesus and still not understand him. Peter said the true words and then tried to talk Jesus out of the cross in the next breath. I do this. I confess him Lord and then flinch when his Lordship leads through suffering, when following means losing rather than gaining. The confession at Caesarea Philippi is not the finish line. It is the place where Jesus turns and sets his face toward Jerusalem, and asks whether the people who named him will follow him there.

**The Christ connection**

He fed thousands in the wilderness, the way God fed Israel with manna, because he is himself the bread that the Father gives. And the bread had to be broken before it could feed anyone. The Christ Peter confessed is the Christ who would let his body be broken and given for the many. To answer the question rightly is to follow a Lord who saves not by avoiding the cross but by carrying it.

You are the Christ.

# Glory on the Mountain, Greatness in the Service
## Mark 9:1-50

Six days after Peter confessed him, Jesus takes three of them up a high mountain, and there his clothing becomes radiant, intensely white, whiter than any launderer could make it. Moses and Elijah appear with him. Peter, terrified and babbling, offers to build three tents, as if this were a moment to capture and keep. Then a cloud overshadows them and a voice speaks, the same voice from the river, but now with a command attached: "This is my beloved Son; listen to him" (Mark 9:7). The Father confirms what Peter confessed. And the command is to listen, because what the Son has been saying about suffering is exactly what Peter does not want to hear.

**The mountain and the valley**

Mark does not let the glory stand alone. They come down the mountain into a mess. The other disciples have failed to cast out a spirit from a boy who convulses and foams. The father's faith is honest and broken: "I believe; help my unbelief" (Mark 9:24). Jesus casts the spirit out and tells the disciples this kind comes out only through prayer. The shining mountain and the failing valley are pressed together on purpose. The glory is real, but the road runs through the valley, and the road runs toward a cross.

**The argument on the road**

Then Jesus tells them a second time, plainly, that he will be delivered into the hands of men and killed and after three days rise. And they do not understand and are afraid to ask. And then, having just heard their Lord predict his own murder, they fall to arguing on the road about which of them is the greatest. Mark places the prediction of the cross next to the squabble over rank so that we cannot miss how grotesque it is. He has to ask them what they were discussing, and they go silent, because they know.

So Jesus sits down, calls the Twelve, and says, "If anyone would be first, he must be last of all and servant of all" (Mark 9:35). Then he takes a child, a person of no status in that world, and puts the child in the middle of them, in his arms, and says that to receive such a one in his name is to receive him, and to receive him is to receive the Father. Greatness in the kingdom is not a higher seat. It is the lowest place and the open arms.

**The cut that follows**

The chapter ends with hard sayings about causing little ones to stumble, about cutting off the hand or foot or eye that leads you to sin, about being salted with fire and having salt in yourselves and being at peace with one another. The seriousness is not random. A people learning to be last and servant of all must be ruthless with the ambition and self-protection that pull them back toward the argument on the road.

This indicts me where I live. I have stood in moments of real spiritual privilege and then, an hour later, kept quiet score of where I rank. The argument about who is greatest is not a problem of the ancient disciples. It is the reflex of every heart that wants the mountain without the valley, the glory without the towel. Jesus does not soften it. He sets a child in front of me and waits.

**The Christ connection**

The One declared beloved Son on the mountain became the servant of all in the valley, and his greatness was proven not on a throne but on a cross, last of all, taking the lowest place there is. The voice said listen to him, and what he says is that the way up is down. He went down first.

First means last and servant.

# A Ransom for Many
## Mark 10:17-52

A man runs up to Jesus and kneels, which is not how the wealthy and respectable usually approach a wandering teacher. "Good Teacher, what must I do to inherit eternal life?" He has kept the commandments from his youth. He is sincere. And Mark records the most tender line in the chapter: "Jesus, looking at him, loved him" (Mark 10:21). Out of that love comes the hardest word. Go, sell what you have, give to the poor, and come, follow me. And the man's face falls, and he goes away sorrowful, because he had great possessions. Jesus let him walk. Love did not soften the demand.

**What the rich man could not release**

The disciples are astonished, because in their world wealth looked like blessing, like proof of God's favor. Jesus tells them how hard it is for the rich to enter the kingdom, harder than a camel through a needle's eye, and when they ask who then can be saved, he gives the answer that frames the whole chapter: "With man it is impossible, but not with God. For all things are possible with God" (Mark 10:27). The man could not let go of his wealth. No one can let go of their idol by sheer effort. Salvation has to come from outside us, from God, or it does not come.

**What James and John tried to grab**

Then the second failure, and it is uglier because it comes from insiders. James and John come to Jesus with a request, having just heard him predict his death a third time, the most detailed yet, mocking and spitting and killing. And what they ask for is the two best seats: grant us to sit at your right and your left in your glory. They want thrones. They are standing next to a man walking toward a cross and asking for cabinet positions. The other ten are indignant, not because the request was wrong but because they wanted the seats too.

**The center of the chapter and the book**

Jesus gathers them and says the sentence everything has been moving toward. The rulers of the nations lord it over people. It shall not be so among you. Whoever would be great must be servant; whoever would be first must be slave of all. And then the reason, the verse that holds the entire Gospel: "For even the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many" (Mark 10:45). A ransom is the price paid to set a captive free. He is not telling them to serve so they can earn a place. He is telling them he will pay with his life what they could never pay, so that the impossible salvation of verse 27 becomes real.

**Where I stand in this chapter**

I would like to be the blind beggar who ends the chapter, Bartimaeus, who throws off his cloak and follows. More often I am the rich man, walking away from the one thing I am told to release, or James and John, asking for honor from the man on his way to die. The chapter does not let me admire the ransom from a safe distance. It puts the price beside my ambition and my grip on what I own, and it asks whether I will follow a Lord whose greatness is a cross.

**The Christ connection**

The rich man could not give up his treasure. The Son of Man gave up everything, his life, as the ransom. He did not ask of us what he was unwilling to do for us, and more, he did what we could never do at all. With man it is impossible. He is the not-impossible. The chapter ends with Bartimaeus seeing and following on the road, the road that leads straight to Jerusalem and the cross where the ransom is paid.

He came to give his life.

# The King Enters and the Tenants Are Judged
## Mark 11:1-12:44

He sends two disciples for a colt that has never been ridden, and rides it into Jerusalem over cloaks and branches while the crowds shout Hosanna and quote the psalm of the coming king. It is a deliberate, staged arrival. The awaited king enters his capital. And then, anticlimactically, Mark says he went into the temple, looked around at everything, and, because it was already late, went back out to Bethany. The king inspects his house. The judgment is coming the next morning.

**The fig tree and the temple**

Mark wraps the temple cleansing inside a strange sign. On the way in, Jesus curses a fig tree that has leaves but no fruit. Then he enters the temple and drives out those buying and selling, overturns the tables, and quotes Isaiah and Jeremiah: "My house shall be called a house of prayer for all the nations? But you have made it a den of robbers" (Mark 11:17). The next morning the fig tree is withered to its roots. The tree is the temple. Leaves without fruit. Religious display covering spiritual barrenness. The king came looking for fruit on his own house and found a market.

**The rejected stone**

Then the authorities challenge him: by what authority do you do these things? And Jesus answers with a parable that is barely a parable. A man plants a vineyard and lets it out to tenants and goes away. At harvest he sends servants for the fruit, and the tenants beat them, kill them, send them away empty. Finally he sends his beloved son, thinking they will respect him. And the tenants say, "This is the heir. Come, let us kill him, and the inheritance will be ours." And they kill him and throw him out of the vineyard.

The leaders understood it perfectly. Mark says they knew he had told the parable against them, and they wanted to arrest him. The vineyard is Israel, the servants are the prophets, the son is Jesus, and the tenants are the men standing in front of him. He is telling them, to their faces, that they are about to kill the heir. And then he quotes the psalm: "The stone that the builders rejected has become the cornerstone" (Mark 12:10). The very One they discard becomes the foundation of everything God is building.

**Missing the One greater than the temple**

The chapters fill with their attempts to trap him, on taxes, on resurrection, on the greatest commandment, and each time he answers with an authority they cannot break. The tragedy underneath all of it is that the men who held the temple, who managed its sacrifices and guarded its courts, could not see that the One the temple pointed to was standing in their courts. They had the building and missed the meaning. The chapters close with a poor widow putting two small coins into the treasury, giving everything, while the wealthy give out of abundance. She is the fruit the temple should have grown. They are the barren tree.

This is the warning I most need. It is possible to spend a life in the courts of the religion and miss the One the religion is about, to defend the building and reject the cornerstone, to be a tenant who treats the vineyard as my own. I can be busy with the house of God and barren before the Son of God. The fig tree had leaves.

**The Christ connection**

The parable is Jesus narrating his own death before it happens. The beloved son thrown out of the vineyard and killed is him, outside the city wall, on a cross. But the quotation that follows turns the murder into the foundation. The rejected stone becomes the cornerstone. They meant his death as the end of his claim. God meant it as the beginning of the new temple, built on the One they threw away.

The rejected stone becomes cornerstone.

# Watch
## Mark 13:1-37

They are leaving the temple, and one of the disciples, like a tourist, points up at the stones: Teacher, look, what wonderful stones and buildings. The temple was one of the wonders of the ancient world, its stones immense, its courts gold-trimmed. And Jesus says the thing no Jewish man wanted to hear: "There will not be left here one stone upon another that will not be thrown down" (Mark 13:2). The disciples admire the architecture. He pronounces its funeral. Within a generation, in AD 70, Rome would do exactly that.

**The question and the warnings**

On the Mount of Olives, looking across at the doomed temple, four of them ask when, and what the sign will be. Jesus answers the whole discourse with a posture more than a timeline. First, the warning that runs through everything: see that no one leads you astray. Many will come claiming his name and deceive many. There will be wars and rumors of wars, earthquakes, famines, but these are the beginning of birth pains, not the end. His followers will be handed over to councils, beaten, dragged before governors, hated for his name. Brother will betray brother. And the gospel must first be proclaimed to all nations.

He speaks of a desolating sacrilege and days of tribulation, of false christs and false prophets performing signs to lead astray, if possible, the elect. And then, beyond the tribulation, the sun darkened, the stars falling, and the Son of Man coming in clouds with great power and glory, gathering his elect from the ends of the earth. The same figure Daniel saw, now identified as the One speaking on the mountain.

**The one command repeated**

What Jesus will not give them is the date. "But concerning that day or that hour, no one knows, not even the angels in heaven, nor the Son, but only the Father" (Mark 13:32). And because the hour is unknown, the whole discourse compresses into a single command, repeated to the end. He tells the parable of the man who goes away from home and leaves his servants in charge, each with work, and commands the doorkeeper to stay awake, because no one knows when the master returns, evening, midnight, cockcrow, or morning. "And what I say to you I say to all: Stay awake" (Mark 13:37).

Notice what watchfulness is not. It is not date-setting. It is not scanning the headlines for the desolating sacrilege. Every generation that has spent its energy calculating the hour has disobeyed the one thing Jesus actually commanded, which was to stay at the work and stay awake. The servant is not told to predict the master's return. He is told to be found doing his job when it comes.

**The cost of watching**

Honest watchfulness is harder than speculation because it has no end date to brace against. It asks me to live every ordinary Tuesday as a man whose Master may return before the kettle boils, to do the assigned work faithfully when no one is checking and no clock is running down. I find it easier to be alarmed by signs than to be faithful in the dark. Alarm feels like devotion. Faithfulness in the long ordinary night is the actual command, and it is the one I most often sleep through.

**The Christ connection**

The Master who tells this parable is about to walk into Gethsemane, where he will ask three friends to watch with him one hour, and find them asleep. Could you not watch one hour? The discourse on watching is immediately tested, and his closest followers fail it. He stayed awake to the cross when everyone else slept. He kept watch for us when we could not keep it for him. And he is coming back, on the clouds, for the servants found awake.

Stay awake. Keep watch.

# The Cross of the Servant King
## Mark 14:1-15:47

A woman breaks an alabaster flask of costly ointment over his head, and the room scolds her for the waste. Jesus defends her: she has anointed his body beforehand for burial. While she pours out everything, Judas, one of the Twelve, goes to the chief priests to sell him. Mark sets the two side by side at the door of the passion, extravagant love and calculated betrayal, and the whole narrative that follows is the collision of those two things.

**Betrayed and denied**

In the upper room he takes bread and a cup and gives them new meaning: this is my body, this is my blood of the covenant, poured out for many. Then Gethsemane, where he falls to the ground and prays that the hour might pass, "Abba, Father, all things are possible for you. Remove this cup from me. Yet not what I will, but what you will" (Mark 14:36). He is not stoic. He is in anguish, and he submits. His friends sleep through it. Judas arrives with a kiss and a crowd, and they all flee. By the courtyard fire Peter, who swore he would die first, denies three times that he even knows the man, and the rooster crows, and Peter weeps.

The One abandoned by every friend goes to trial alone. Before the council, when asked directly if he is the Christ, the Son of the Blessed, he answers plainly, "I am," and they condemn him for blasphemy. Before Pilate the crowd that shouted Hosanna days earlier now shouts crucify. He is mocked, spit on, crowned with thorns, dressed in purple by soldiers who kneel in cruel parody before the King.

**The death and the torn curtain**

They crucify him, and the mockery continues at the cross: he saved others, he cannot save himself; let the Christ come down now that we may see and believe. They do not understand that he could not save himself precisely because he was saving them. Darkness covers the land. And he cries out the opening line of Psalm 22, "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?", the Son tasting the abandonment we earned. Then he breathes his last.

And Mark records two things at the moment of death. First: "the curtain of the temple was torn in two, from top to bottom" (Mark 15:38). The veil that walled off the Holy of Holies, that kept sinners out of God's presence, is torn open, from the top, by God, the moment the ransom is paid. The way in is opened by his dying. Second, the centurion standing facing him, watching how he died, says, "Truly this man was the Son of God." A Roman executioner, a Gentile, confesses at the cross exactly what Mark wrote in his first verse. The Son of God is recognized, finally and fully, not in glory but in death.

**Where I am in the courtyard**

I want to believe I would have stood by him. But Mark gives me Peter at the fire, and I know that man. He loved Jesus genuinely and denied him for fear of a servant girl's question. The distance between my sworn loyalty and my actual courage is the distance between the upper room and the courtyard, and I have walked it. The cross does not flatter me. It shows me a Savior abandoned by the very people who meant it most, and tells me he died for them anyway.

**The Christ connection**

Everything Mark has built points here. The authority to forgive, the ransom for many, the rejected stone, the Son of Man who came to serve, all of it lands at this cross. He was forsaken so that I would never be. The curtain tore so that I could come in. The verdict announced in verse one is sealed in blood and confessed by an enemy soldier.

Truly this was God's Son.

# He Has Risen; He Is Not Here
## Mark 16:1-8

Very early on the first day of the week, when the sun had risen, three women walk to a tomb carrying spices to anoint a dead body. They have one practical worry: "Who will roll away the stone for us from the entrance of the tomb?" (Mark 16:3). They are not expecting a resurrection. They are expecting a corpse, and a problem getting to it. This is the honest grief of people who watched him die and came to do the last sad thing love can do for the dead.

**The stone already moved**

Then they look up, and the stone, which was very large, has already been rolled back. They enter and find a young man dressed in white sitting on the right side, and they are alarmed. And he speaks the sentence the whole Gospel has been driving toward: "You seek Jesus of Nazareth, who was crucified. He has risen; he is not here. See the place where they laid him" (Mark 16:6). He does not soften the crucifixion. He names it, the crucified one, and then he announces the impossible: he is risen. The grave that held everyone could not hold him. The women came to anoint a body and found an empty shelf.

**Go, tell, he goes before you**

The young man does not let them stand there. He gives them a commission. Go, tell his disciples and Peter, and notice that Peter is named, the one who denied him, singled out for grace, that he is going before you to Galilee. There you will see him, just as he told you. The risen Lord is not a static fact to verify. He is already moving ahead of them, calling them to follow again to the place where it all began.

**The abrupt ending**

And then Mark ends, in the oldest manuscripts, with one of the strangest verses in the New Testament. "And they went out and fled from the tomb, for trembling and astonishment had seized them, and they said nothing to anyone, for they were afraid" (Mark 16:8). No appearance of the risen Jesus. No triumphant proclamation. Just three frightened women running in silence. The Gospel that opened with a confident verdict ends mid-breath, on fear.

Many have found this ending unsatisfying, and ancient scribes added longer endings to round it off. But Mark may have known exactly what he was doing. He ends on the women's failure to speak so that the reader is left holding the unfinished sentence. The angel said go and tell, and they were afraid and said nothing. The story is incomplete on the page because it is meant to be completed in you. Will you do what they could not yet do? Will you believe the word and go?

**Where this leaves me**

I recognize myself in that silence more than I would like. I have stood with the news of the risen Christ in my hands and been seized by fear of what saying it out loud would cost, and gone quiet. Mark refuses to let me read the resurrection as a tidy happy ending I observe from a safe seat. He ends the sentence in my throat. The empty tomb is not a fact to admire. It is a command to obey, and a Lord already gone on ahead, waiting in Galilee.

**The Christ connection**

The crucified One is risen, and that single fact validates everything Mark wrote from verse one. The ransom was accepted. The rejected stone is vindicated as the cornerstone. The Son of God who died forsaken is alive and going before his people, including the one who denied him by name. He does not wait at the tomb for us to come find him. He goes ahead, and calls us to follow into the world with the word the women were first too afraid to say.

He is going before you.
